decks.title: Upthrust and Archimedes’ Principle — Part 1: Upthrust, apparent weight and relative density
goals: Explain why a body seems lighter in a liquid and state the factors on which upthrust depends
State Archimedes’ principle and calculate upthrust and apparent weight
Calculate relative density from weights in air and in water, and describe how it is measured

slides.heading: Why do we feel lighter in water?
slides.body_md: Part 1 — a liquid pushes upwards on everything placed in it.

visual.alt: Flow from a body placed in a liquid to the liquid pushing up to the body seeming lighter

slides.narration: A bucket of water is heavy in the air, yet a large stone is easy to lift under water. The water is helping you. That upward help from a liquid is the subject of this chapter.

slides.heading: Buoyancy and upthrust
slides.body_md: A liquid exerts an **upward force** on a body placed in it. This force is called **upthrust** (or **buoyant force**), and the property of a liquid to exert it is **buoyancy**. It acts **vertically upwards**, against the weight of the body.

rows: The pressure of the liquid is greater on the lower face than on the upper face
The body seems to weigh less in the liquid

visual.alt: Table of four properties of upthrust

slides.narration: Upthrust always acts straight up. It arises because pressure in a liquid grows with depth, so the push from below is bigger than the push from above. The result is that the body seems lighter.

slides.heading: A body in air and in water
slides.body_md: A spring balance shows 15 N when the body hangs in air. With the body **fully in water** it shows only 9 N. The weight has not changed; the **upthrust of 6 N** acts upwards.

slides.heading: Archimedes’ principle
slides.body_md: When a body is **fully or partly immersed** in a fluid, it experiences an upthrust **equal to the weight of the fluid displaced** by it. Upthrust $= V \rho g$, where $V$ is the volume immersed and $\rho$ is the density of the liquid.

slides.narration: Archimedes found that the upthrust equals the weight of the liquid pushed aside. In the overflow can, the water that spills into the beaker is exactly the water the body displaced, and its weight equals the upthrust.

slides.heading: Apparent weight
slides.body_md: The weight of a body in a liquid is called its **apparent weight**. If the upthrust is **less than the weight**, the body sinks and its apparent weight is positive: **apparent weight = weight in air − upthrust**.

visual.alt: Table of weight in air, upthrust and apparent weight

slides.narration: Apparent weight is what a spring balance reads when the body is in the liquid. It equals the weight in air minus the upthrust, so it is always smaller than the true weight.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: upthrust and apparent weight
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A body of volume 600 cm³ weighs 15 N in air. It is fully immersed in water. Find the upthrust and the apparent weight. ($\rho = 1000$ kg m⁻³, $g = 10$ m s⁻²)

**Step 1.** $V = 600 \times 10^{-6} = 0.0006$ m³. Upthrust $= V \rho g = 0.0006 \times 1000 \times 10 = 6$ N.

**Step 2.** Apparent weight $= 15 - 6 = 9$ N.

visual.alt: Table of the working for the upthrust and the apparent weight

slides.narration: Change the volume to cubic metres. Multiply volume, density and gee to get the upthrust, six newtons. Subtract it from the weight in air, fifteen newtons, to get the apparent weight, nine newtons.

slides.heading: Quick check: finding the upthrust
slides.body_md: Use upthrust = V ρ g with the volume in cubic metres.

visual.alt: Table of the volume and the liquid in the check question

slides.narration: A body of volume two hundred and fifty cubic centimetres is fully immersed in water. What is the upthrust on it?

slides.heading: What upthrust depends on
slides.body_md: Upthrust depends on the **volume of the body immersed**, the **density of the liquid** and $g$. It does **not** depend on the weight, density or material of the body, nor on the depth once the body is fully immersed.

rows: Density or material of the body

visual.alt: Table of the factors that upthrust does and does not depend on

slides.narration: Two bodies of equal volume, one of iron and one of wood, feel the same upthrust when fully under water. Only the volume pushed aside and the density of the liquid matter. Going deeper does not change it.

slides.heading: Density and relative density
slides.body_md: **Relative density (RD)** of a substance is the ratio of its **density** to the density of **water**. It is a pure ratio with **no unit**. The density in kg m⁻³ is RD × 1000.

visual.alt: Table of relative densities and densities of five substances

slides.narration: Relative density compares a substance with water. Iron is seven point eight times as dense as water, mercury thirteen point six times. Because it is a ratio, it has no unit. Multiply by one thousand to get the density.

slides.heading: Finding the RD of a solid denser than water
slides.body_md: Weigh the solid in air and then fully in water with a spring balance. Upthrust $=$ weight of an equal volume of water $= W_{\text{air}} - W_{\text{water}}$. So $\text{RD} = \dfrac{W_{\text{air}}}{W_{\text{air}} - W_{\text{water}}}$.

rows: Weight of an equal volume of water

visual.alt: Table of the three readings used to find the relative density of a solid

slides.narration: The loss of weight in water equals the weight of the same volume of water. Divide the weight of the solid by that loss and you have its relative density. Only a spring balance and a beaker of water are needed.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: relative density of a metal piece
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A metal piece weighs 8 N in air and 5 N in water. Find its relative density and its density.

**Step 1.** Loss of weight $= 8 - 5 = 3$ N.

**Step 2.** $\text{RD} = \dfrac{8}{3} = 2.67$, so the density is $2.67 \times 1000 = 2670$ kg m⁻³.

visual.alt: Table of the working for the relative density and density of the metal piece

slides.narration: Subtract the two readings to get the loss of weight, three newtons. Divide the weight in air by this loss to find the relative density, about two point six seven. Multiply by one thousand for the density.

slides.body_md: A solid weighs 6 N in air and 4 N in water.

visual.alt: Table of the weights of a solid in air and in water

slides.narration: A solid weighs six newtons in air and four newtons in water. What is its relative density?

slides.heading: Finding the RD of a liquid
slides.body_md: Use one solid that sinks in both liquids. Weigh it in air, in water and in the liquid. $\text{RD of liquid} = \dfrac{W_{\text{air}} - W_{\text{liquid}}}{W_{\text{air}} - W_{\text{water}}}$. Example: 6 N, 4 N and 4.4 N give 0.8.

visual.alt: Table of the readings and the relative density of the liquid

slides.narration: For a liquid, compare the loss of weight in that liquid with the loss in water. Both are upthrusts on the same solid, so their ratio is the ratio of the densities, the relative density of the liquid.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Upthrust is the upward force of a liquid on a body; it acts vertically upwards.
Archimedes’ principle: upthrust = weight of the liquid displaced = V ρ g.
Apparent weight = weight in air − upthrust.
RD of a solid = W(air) ÷ [W(air) − W(water)]; RD of a liquid = [W(air) − W(liquid)] ÷ [W(air) − W(water)].

visual.alt: Summary table of upthrust, apparent weight and relative density

slides.narration: To sum up Part one. Upthrust is the upward push of a liquid. It equals the weight of liquid displaced. The apparent weight is the weight in air minus the upthrust, and relative density is found from weights in air and in water.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Convert cm³ to m³ before using V ρ g: 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³.
Say "weight of liquid displaced" when stating Archimedes’ principle.
Relative density has no unit; density has kg m⁻³.
In RD problems, subtract first to find the loss of weight.

rows: Using the weight of the body as the upthrust
Upthrust is the weight of liquid displaced
Using volume in cm³ with ρ in kg m⁻³

slides.heading: Why does a steel ship float?
slides.body_md: Part 2 — sinking, floating and the law that decides between them.

visual.alt: Flow from the weight of the body compared with the upthrust to sinking or floating

slides.narration: A steel nail sinks at once, yet a ship made of tonnes of steel floats. The same liquid and the same metal give two different results. The answer lies in comparing weight and upthrust.

slides.heading: Sink, float or rise?
slides.body_md: Compare the **weight** $W$ with the **upthrust** $U$ of a fully immersed body. A denser body sinks, a body of equal density stays where it is placed, and a less dense body rises and floats.

headers: Density of body compared with the liquid

visual.alt: Table of the three cases of sinking, floating fully immersed and rising to float

slides.narration: If the upthrust is smaller than the weight, the body sinks. If they are equal, it floats fully under the surface. If the upthrust would be larger, the body rises until part of it is out of the liquid.

slides.heading: Three cases in pictures
slides.body_md: In the **third case** the body floats with part above the surface, so it displaces less liquid than its full volume, until the upthrust **equals its weight**.

slides.body_md: A floating body displaces its own **weight** of liquid: **weight of the floating body = weight of the liquid displaced** (the upthrust). A heavier floating body therefore sinks lower.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a floating log

**Problem.** A pine log of density 650 kg m⁻³ floats in water. What percentage of its volume is below the surface, and what percentage is above?

**Step 1.** $\dfrac{V_{\text{in}}}{V} = \dfrac{650}{1000} = 0.65$, that is 65% below.

**Step 2.** Above the surface: $100 - 65 = 35$%.

slides.heading: Ships

notes.title: Upthrust and Archimedes’ Principle — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Buoyancy and upthrust
sections.body_md:
A liquid exerts an **upward force** on a body placed in it. This force is the **upthrust** (buoyant force); the property of a liquid to exert it is **buoyancy**. SI unit: newton.

- It acts **vertically upwards** through the centre of gravity of the liquid displaced (the centre of buoyancy). It arises because the pressure on the lower face of the body is greater than on the upper face.
- A body seems **lighter** in a liquid: a spring balance reads 15 N for a body in air and 9 N when it is fully in water, because of an upthrust of 6 N.
- **Upthrust depends on** the volume of the body that is immersed, the density of the liquid and $g$. It does **not** depend on the weight, density or material of the body, or (once the body is fully immersed) on the depth.

key_terms.definition_md: The upward force exerted by a liquid on a body immersed in it; also called the buoyant force.
The property of a liquid by which it exerts an upward force on a body placed in it.

sections.heading: 2. Archimedes’ principle and apparent weight
sections.body_md:
**Archimedes’ principle:** when a body is fully or partly immersed in a fluid, it experiences an upthrust equal to the **weight of the fluid displaced** by it.

Upthrust $U = V \rho g$ with $V$ the volume immersed (in m³; $1\ \text{cm}^3 = 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^3$), $\rho$ the density of the liquid.

**Apparent weight** is the weight of the body in the liquid. When the upthrust is **less than the weight**, the body sinks and
apparent weight $=$ weight in air $-$ upthrust.

**Verification:** a body hangs from a spring balance in an overflow can; the water that overflows into a beaker is collected and weighed; its weight equals the loss of weight of the body (the upthrust).

key_terms.definition_md: A body immersed in a fluid experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.
The weight of a body when immersed in a liquid; weight in air minus the upthrust.

sections.heading: 3. Relative density
sections.body_md:
**Relative density (RD)** of a substance = density of the substance ÷ density of water. It is a ratio and has **no unit**. Density in kg m⁻³ $=$ RD $\times$ 1000.

**RD of a solid denser than water** (spring balance, solid insoluble in water): weigh it in air ($W_1$) and fully in water ($W_2$). The loss of weight $W_1 - W_2$ is the weight of an equal volume of water, so $\text{RD} = \dfrac{W_1}{W_1 - W_2}$.

**RD of a liquid:** weigh a solid that sinks in both liquids in air ($W_1$), in water ($W_2$) and in the liquid ($W_3$): $\text{RD of the liquid} = \dfrac{W_1 - W_3}{W_1 - W_2}$.

key_terms.definition_md: The ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water at 4 °C; it has no unit.

sections.heading: 4. Floatation
sections.body_md:
A body of density $\rho_b$ in a liquid of density $\rho_l$:

| Condition | Result |
|---|---|
| $\rho_b > \rho_l$ (U less than W) | **Sinks**; apparent weight = W − U |
| $\rho_b = \rho_l$ (U = W) | **Floats fully immersed** at any depth |
| $\rho_b < \rho_l$ | Rises and **floats partly immersed**, with U = W for the immersed volume |

**Law of floatation:** a floating body displaces its own weight of liquid: weight of the body = weight of the liquid displaced = upthrust.

**Fraction immersed:** $\dfrac{V_{\text{in}}}{V} = \dfrac{\rho_b}{\rho_l}$. In water, a body of density 600 kg m⁻³ floats with 60% of its volume below the surface.

key_terms.definition_md: A floating body displaces a weight of liquid equal to its own weight.

sections.heading: 5. Applications: ships, submarines, icebergs and balloons
sections.body_md:
- **Ship:** an iron ship is hollow, so it displaces a very large weight of water; its **average density** is less than that of water and the upthrust equals its weight. A **Plimsoll line** marks how low a ship may float safely in different waters.
- **Submarine:** it has **ballast tanks**. Filling them with sea water increases its weight (and average density) so it **dives**; blowing the water out with compressed air makes it **rise**. To stay at one depth its average density equals that of the water.
- **Iceberg:** ice (about 900 kg m⁻³) is slightly less dense than sea water (about 1030 kg m⁻³), so about 87.4% of the volume is below the surface and only about 12.6% above it.
- **Balloon:** filled with a gas (hot air, hydrogen or helium) less dense than the surrounding air; it rises while the upthrust $V \rho_{\text{air}} g$ exceeds its total weight, and stops where the two are equal.

Densities are approximate and differ slightly between books; each question states the values it uses.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using the volume in cm³ with density in kg m⁻³ and g in m s⁻² without converting.
- Taking the weight of the body as the upthrust when the body is sinking.
- Giving relative density a unit.
- Using the whole volume of a floating body in V ρ g instead of the volume immersed.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Statements (2 marks): Archimedes' principle with "weight of liquid displaced"; the law of floatation.
- Numericals (1 to 3 marks): formula, substitution with units, answer with unit.
- Applications (2 to 3 marks): average density for a ship, ballast tanks for a submarine, the ratio of densities for an iceberg.

questions.stem_md: Describe how you would find the relative density of a solid that is denser than water, using a spring balance and a beaker of water. State the readings and the formula.

answer.model_answer_md: Hang the solid from a spring balance and note its weight in air, **W₁**. Lower it fully into the water, without touching the beaker, and note the reading **W₂**. The loss of weight, W₁ − W₂, is the weight of an equal volume of water. Then $\text{RD} = \dfrac{W_1}{W_1 - W_2}$.

questions.solution_md: W₁ in air, W₂ in water; RD = W₁ / (W₁ − W₂).

questions.stem_md: A metal piece weighs 5 N in air and 3 N in water. Find its relative density.
A solid weighs 6 N in air, 4 N in water and 4.5 N in a liquid. Find the relative density of the liquid.
The relative density of a metal is 8.9. Find its density in kg m⁻³.
questions.solution_md: $\rho = \text{RD} \times 1000 = 8.9 \times 1000 = 8900$ kg m⁻³.

questions.stem_md: Why does a steel needle sink in water but a large steel ship floats?

answer.model_answer_md: The needle is **solid steel**, much denser than water, so it sinks. The ship is **hollow**; its large volume displaces a very large weight of water and its **average density is less than that of water**.

questions.stem_md: A wooden block of mass 0.6 kg and volume 1000 cm³ is placed in water. (a) Show that it floats. (b) Find the volume of the block below the surface. (Density of water 1000 kg m⁻³; g = 10 m s⁻²)

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Density $= \dfrac{0.6}{0.001} = 600$ kg m⁻³, which is **less than 1000 kg m⁻³**, so the block floats.

**(b)** For floating, upthrust $=$ weight $= 0.6 \times 10 = 6$ N. $V_{\text{in}} = \dfrac{6}{1000 \times 10} = 0.0006$ m³, that is **600 cm³**.

questions.solution_md: Density 600 kg m⁻³ is below 1000; volume below the surface 600 cm³.

questions.stem_md: A block of wood of density 600 kg m⁻³ and volume 500 cm³ floats in water. Find the volume of the block above the surface of the water. (Density of water 1000 kg m⁻³)
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{V_{\text{in}}}{V} = \dfrac{600}{1000} = 0.6$, so $V_{\text{in}} = 0.6 \times 500 = 300$ cm³ and the volume above is $500 - 300 = 200$ cm³.

questions.stem_md: A small object of volume 200 cm³ floats fully immersed in brine of density 1200 kg m⁻³. Find its mass. (g = 10 m s⁻²)
questions.solution_md: For floating, weight $=$ upthrust $= V \rho g = 200 \times 10^{-6} \times 1200 \times 10 = 2.4$ N, so $m = \dfrac{W}{g} = \dfrac{2.4}{10} = 0.24$ kg.

questions.stem_md: Ice of density 920 kg m⁻³ floats in sea water of density 1030 kg m⁻³. Find the percentage of the volume of the ice that is below the surface.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{V_{\text{in}}}{V} \times 100 = \dfrac{920}{1030} \times 100 = 89.3$ %.

questions.stem_md: A boat of mass 800 kg floats in river water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. Find the volume of water the boat displaces.
questions.solution_md: A floating body displaces its own weight of water, so the mass of water displaced is 800 kg and $V = \dfrac{m}{\rho} = \dfrac{800}{1000} = 0.8$ m³.

questions.stem_md: A piece of cork of density 240 kg m⁻³ floats in water. Find the percentage of its volume that is above the surface. (Density of water 1000 kg m⁻³)
questions.solution_md: Below the surface: $\dfrac{240}{1000} \times 100 = 24$ %, so above the surface: $100 - 24 = 76$ %.

questions.stem_md: Explain how a submarine dives and how it returns to the surface.

answer.model_answer_md: To **dive**, water is let into its **ballast tanks**, which increases its weight and average density. To **surface**, **compressed air** pushes the water out, making it lighter than the water it displaces.

questions.solution_md: Ballast tanks filled with water to dive; emptied with compressed air to rise.

questions.stem_md: Explain why a balloon filled with hot air rises, and why it stops rising at a certain height.

answer.model_answer_md: Hot air is **less dense** than the cooler air outside, so the **upthrust**, which equals the weight of the air displaced, is **greater than the total weight** of the balloon and it rises. Higher up the air is thinner, so the upthrust falls. At the height where the **upthrust equals the weight**, the balloon stops rising.

questions.solution_md: Hot air is less dense so upthrust exceeds weight; upthrust falls with height; it stops where they are equal.

marking_scheme.step: Less dense gas, upthrust greater than weight
Upthrust falls as the air thins

The figure shows the same body hanging from a spring balance, first in air (left) and then fully immersed in water (right). The parts on the right are lettered A to E, and the scales are marked in newton. (Density of water 1000 kg m⁻³; g = 10 m s⁻²)

(a) Name the parts A, B, C, D and E. [3]

(b) Read from the scales the weight of the body in air and its apparent weight in water. [2]

(c) Find the upthrust on the body and the volume of the body. [3]

(d) State Archimedes’ principle. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **A** is the spring balance; **B** is the body; **C** is the water; **D** is the upthrust (upward arrow); **E** is the weight of the body (downward arrow).

**(b)** Weight in air = **15 N**; apparent weight in water = **9 N**.

**(c)** Upthrust $= 15 - 9 = 6$ N. Volume $V = \dfrac{U}{\rho g} = \dfrac{6}{1000 \times 10} = 0.0006$ m³, that is **600 cm³**.

**(d)** When a body is wholly or partly immersed in a fluid, the **upthrust** on it is **equal to the weight of the fluid displaced** by it.

questions.solution_md: Balance, body, water, upthrust, weight; 15 N and 9 N; 6 N and 600 cm³; Archimedes’ principle.

marking_scheme.step: Upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced

questions.stem_md:
A student weighs a metal piece with a spring balance. It weighs 4.8 N in air, 4 N when fully immersed in water, and 4.2 N when fully immersed in a liquid X. (Density of water 1000 kg m⁻³)

(a) Define relative density. [2]

(b) Find the loss of weight in water and state what it equals. [2]

(c) Find the relative density of the metal and its density. [3]

(d) Find the relative density of liquid X. [2]

(e) State one precaution to be taken while the piece is in the water. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The **ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water**; it has no unit.

**(b)** Loss of weight $= 4.8 - 4 = 0.8$ N, which equals the **weight of an equal volume of water** (the upthrust).

**(c)** $\text{RD} = \dfrac{4.8}{0.8} = 6$, so the density is $6 \times 1000 = 6000$ kg m⁻³.

**(d)** $\text{RD of X} = \dfrac{4.8 - 4.2}{4.8 - 4} = \dfrac{0.6}{0.8} = 0.75$.

**(e)** The piece must be **completely under water without touching the sides or bottom** of the beaker (and free of air bubbles).

questions.solution_md: Ratio of densities; 0.8 N, weight of equal volume of water; RD 6 and 6000 kg m⁻³; 0.75; keep the piece fully immersed and clear of the beaker.

marking_scheme.step: Ratio to the density of water
Equals the weight of an equal volume of water

questions.stem_md:
Three blocks A, B and C, each of volume 500 cm³, have densities 2500 kg m⁻³, 1000 kg m⁻³ and 400 kg m⁻³. Each is released gently in water. (Density of water 1000 kg m⁻³; g = 10 m s⁻²)

(a) State what each block does (sinks, floats fully immersed or floats partly immersed), with a reason. [3]

(b) Find the weight of each block. [3]

(c) Find the apparent weight of the block that sinks. [2]

(d) Find the volume of the floating block C that is below the surface. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **A** sinks, because its density is greater than that of water. **B** floats fully immersed, because its density equals that of water. **C** floats partly immersed, because its density is less than that of water.

**(b)** $W = V \rho g$: A $= 0.0005 \times 2500 \times 10 = 12.5$ N; B $= 0.0005 \times 1000 \times 10 = 5$ N; C $= 0.0005 \times 400 \times 10 = 2$ N.

**(c)** Upthrust on A (fully immersed) $= 0.0005 \times 1000 \times 10 = 5$ N, so the apparent weight $= 12.5 - 5 = 7.5$ N.

**(d)** C floats, so upthrust $=$ weight $= 2$ N, and $V_{\text{in}} = \dfrac{2}{1000 \times 10} = 0.0002$ m³, that is **200 cm³**.

questions.solution_md: A sinks, B floats fully immersed, C floats partly; 12.5 N, 5 N, 2 N; 7.5 N; 200 cm³.

marking_scheme.step: B floats fully immersed with reason
C floats partly immersed with reason

questions.stem_md:
An iceberg floats in the sea. (Density of ice 900 kg m⁻³; of sea water 1030 kg m⁻³; of fresh water 1000 kg m⁻³)

(a) Explain why only a small part of the iceberg is seen above the surface. [2]

(b) Find the percentage of the volume of the iceberg that is below the surface and the percentage that is above it. [3]

(c) The iceberg has a total volume of 20 000 m³. Find the volume above the surface. [2]

(d) Find the percentage of the volume of the same ice below the surface when it floats in fresh water. [2]

(e) Name the law of floatation used to answer (b). [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Ice is **only slightly less dense** than sea water, so it floats with almost all of its volume **immersed**; the part above the surface is small.

**(b)** $\dfrac{V_{\text{in}}}{V} = \dfrac{900}{1030} = 0.874$, so **87.4%** is below the surface and $100 - 87.4 = $ **12.6%** is above it.

**(c)** Volume above $= 20000 \times 0.126 = 2520$ m³ (about).

**(d)** $\dfrac{900}{1000} \times 100 = 90$ %.

**(e)** The **law of floatation**: a floating body displaces its own weight of liquid.

questions.solution_md: Ice is slightly less dense; 87.4% below and 12.6% above; about 2520 m³; 90%; law of floatation.

marking_scheme.step: Ice slightly less dense than sea water
Most of the volume is immersed

questions.stem_md:
A submarine has a volume of 3000 m³. When floating on the surface of the sea its weight is 2.4 × 10⁷ N. (Density of sea water 1030 kg m⁻³; g = 10 m s⁻²)

(a) Find the volume of the submarine below the surface when it floats, and this as a percentage of its total volume. [3]

(b) Find the upthrust on it when it is fully submerged. [2]

(c) Find the weight of water that must be taken into the ballast tanks for it to be just fully submerged and to float at one depth. [2]

(d) Describe how it returns to the surface. [2]

(e) State whether the upthrust changes as it dives deeper, with a reason. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Floating: upthrust $=$ weight, so $V_{\text{in}} = \dfrac{24000000}{1030 \times 10} = 2330$ m³ (about), that is $\dfrac{2330}{3000} \times 100 = 77.7$ %.

**(b)** $U = V \rho g = 3000 \times 1030 \times 10 = 30900000$ N.

**(c)** Extra weight $= 30900000 - 24000000 = 6900000$ N, which is the weight of **690000 kg** of sea water (about).

**(d)** **Compressed air** is used to force water out of the ballast tanks, so the weight and average density fall and the upthrust exceeds the weight.

**(e)** The upthrust **does not change**, because the volume displaced and the density of the water stay the same (once fully submerged).

questions.stem_md:
A balloon of volume 600 m³ is filled with helium of density 0.18 kg m⁻³. The air around it has density 1.2 kg m⁻³. The envelope, basket and load together weigh 3000 N. (g = 10 m s⁻²)

(a) Find the upthrust on the balloon. [2]

(b) Find the weight of the helium in it. [2]

(c) Find the net upward force on the balloon when it is released, and the extra mass it could carry and still just rise. [3]

(d) Explain why the balloon stops rising at a great height. [2]

(e) State the condition for the balloon to hover. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $U = V \rho_{\text{air}} g = 600 \times 1.2 \times 10 = 7200$ N.

**(b)** $W_{\text{He}} = 600 \times 0.18 \times 10 = 1080$ N.

**(c)** Net force $= 7200 - 1080 - 3000 = 3120$ N upwards. A load of weight 3120 N has a mass of $\dfrac{3120}{10} = 312$ kg.

**(d)** The air gets **thinner (less dense)** at greater heights, so the upthrust, which is the weight of the air displaced, **falls** until it equals the total weight.

**(e)** The upthrust equals the total weight of the balloon, its gas and its load.
